label: asp:sutva
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{asp:sutva}
		Let $\bm{Y}_{ij}(A_i,\allowbreak \bm{A}_{-i})$ denote the potential outcome for individual $j$ in cluster $i$ given assignments across all clusters, and $\bm{A}_{-i}$ denote the vector of assignments for all other clusters, then (i) $\bm{Y}_{ij}(A_i,\bm{A}_{-i}) = \bm{Y}_{ij}(A_i,\bm{A}_{-i}^*)$ for all $\bm{A}_{-i}\neq \bm{A}_{-i}^*$; and (ii) $\bm{Y}_{ij}(A_i,\bm{A}_{-i}) = \bm{Y}_{ij}(A_i^*,\bm{A}_{-i}^*)$ if $A_i=A_i^*$.
head: environment
name: Cluster-level SUTVA

label: ex:non-prioritized
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:non-prioritized} 
		The non-prioritized setting involves multiple outcomes that do not admit a hierarchical order of importance, i.e., the $Q$ outcomes $(Y_1,\ldots,Y_Q)$ are compared simultaneously rather than sequentially. For example, consider a socioeconomic investigation in which the primary outcomes of interest include income per unit time ($Y_1$), satisfaction with the working environment ($Y_2$), and overall quality of life ($Y_3$), and the intervention under study is a specific employment training program. In this context, the effectiveness of the intervention is evaluated based on an aggregate summary of the comparative results for $(Y_1, Y_2, Y_3)$ between the two groups. Accordingly, for each outcome $Y_q$ that is measured on a different scale, one may specify an outcome-specific contrast based on, for instance, the Heaviside step function $w_q(u_q, v_q) = \mathbbm{1}(u_q > v_q) + 0.5 \mathbbm{1}(u_q = v_q)- \mathbbm{1}(u_q < v_q)$. The overall contrast function can then be defined as $w(\bm{u}, \bm{v}) = \sum_{q=1}^3 \omega_q w_q(u_q, v_q)$, where $\omega_q$ quantifies the pre-specified relative contribution of each outcome to the overall assessment.
head: environment
name: \emph{Non-prioritized, dimension-wise comparison}

label: ex:prioritized
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:prioritized}
		With prioritized outcomes, a consensus-based hierarchical ordering of importance is imposed on $(Y_1,\ldots,Y_Q)$. For example, in a time-to-event clinical trial, the time to the most important event ($Y_1$), e.g., death, is used to determine the ``winner.'' If this comparison is inconclusive (for instance, if neither patient experiences death during their shared follow-up period), the comparison proceeds to the times to the second most important event ($Y_2$), e.g., hospitalization, and so forth. This hierarchy of clinical importance among events can be formally represented through a joint comparison contrast function $w(\bm{u},\bm{v}) = \mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} \succ \bm{v})$, where `$\succ$' denotes a user-specified partial order, and $\bm{u} \succ \bm{v}$ indicates that outcome vector $\bm{u}$ is more favorable than outcome vector $\bm{v}$ \citep{bebu2016large}. Specifically, with $Q=2$ and $(Y_1,Y_2)$, one can define this partial order as $w(\bm{u},\bm{v}) = \mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} \succ \bm{v}) \equiv \mathbbm{1}(u_1>v_1) + \mathbbm{1}(u_1=v_1)\mathbbm{1}(u_2>v_2)$.
head: environment
name: \emph{Prioritized, joint comparison}

label: ex:pareto
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:pareto}
		The Pareto partial order defines a relationship where one element ``Pareto dominates'' another if it's superior in at least one criterion and not worse in any other, thus creating a partial ordering (but not in a sequential comparison scheme) with some options remaining incomparable. For example, in a smoking cessation study comparing two intervention strategies, lung cancer incidence ($Y_1$), nicotine dependence severity ($Y_2$), and healthcare costs ($Y_3$) can be of joint interest. Under a Pareto partial order, one intervention is deemed preferable to another if it exhibits a strictly superior value in at least one of the three outcomes, while being no worse in any of the remaining. In this case, the contrast function $w(\bm{u},\bm{v})=\mathbbm{1}(\bm{u}\preceq_P\bm{v})$, where $\mathbbm{1}(\bm{u}\preceq_P\bm{v})=1$ if $u_q\leq v_q$ for all $q=1,2,3$ and $u_q< v_q$ for some $q=1,2,3$, and $\mathbbm{1}(\bm{u}\preceq_P\bm{v})=0$ otherwise.
head: environment
name: \emph{Non-prioritized, joint comparison}

label: rmk:estimand
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:estimand}
		Our generalized causal effect estimands serve as building blocks for a broader class of summary causal estimands of the form $\Lambda = f(\lambda_1,\lambda_0)$, where $f(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a known function defining the scale of measure. Suppose the contrast function $w(\bm{u},\bm{v}) = \mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} \succ \bm{v})$ defines a partial order as in Example \ref{ex:prioritized}. If we specify $f(u,v)=u-v$, then $\Lambda_C=\lambda_{C,1}-\lambda_{C,0}$ and $\Lambda_I=\lambda_{I,1}-\lambda_{I,0}$ become the cluster-pair and individual-pair net benefit estimands. If we specify $f(u,v)=u/v$, $\Lambda_C=\lambda_{C,1}/\lambda_{C,0}$ and $\Lambda_I=\lambda_{I,1}/\lambda_{I,0}$ become the cluster-pair and individual-pair win ratio estimands. Furthermore, if we modify the contrast function to account for ties $w(\bm{u},\bm{v}) = \mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} \succeq \bm{v})=\mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} \succ \bm{v})+0.5 \mathbbm{1}(\bm{u} =\bm{v})$ and set $f(u,v)=u/v$, then $\Lambda_C=\lambda_{C,1}/\lambda_{C,0}$ and $\Lambda_I=\lambda_{I,1}/\lambda_{I,0}$ become the cluster-pair and individual-pair win odds estimands. These estimands extend their counterparts defined for independent data \citep{buyse2010generalized,bebu2016large,brunner2021win} to the CRT setting.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: When $Q=1$ and a single outcome is considered, our estimands nest two special cases. First, if we specify the contrast function as a difference function $w(Y_{ij},Y_{kl})=Y_{ij}-Y_{kl}$, then $\lambda_{C,a}$ and $\lambda_{I,a}$ reduce to the conventional cluster-average and individual-average treatment effect estimands \citep{kahan2023estimands}. Second, if we specify the contrast as $w(Y_{ij},Y_{kl})=\mathbbm{1}(Y_{ij}>Y_{kl})+0.5\mathbbm{1}(Y_{ij}=Y_{kl})$, then $\lambda_{C,a}$ and $\lambda_{I,a}$ become the cluster-average and individual-average probabilistic index estimands, generalizing the counterpart used previously for independent data \citep{thas2012probabilistic}.
head: environment

label: asp:super-pop
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{asp:super-pop}
		(i) $\mathcal{D}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{D}_m$ are mutually independent. (ii) The unknown cluster size distribution $\mathcal{P}(N)$ is defined over a finite support on $\mathbb{N}^+$. (iii) Given $N_i$, $\mathcal{D}_i$ follows an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{D}|N)$ with finite second moments.
head: environment
name: Population distributions

label: asp:cl-ran
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{asp:cl-ran}
		For cluster $i$, the treatment indicator $A_i$ is an independent draw from the Bernoulli distribution $\mathcal{P}(A)$ with known parameter $\mathbb{P}(A_i = 1) = \pi\in(0, 1)$. Furthermore, $A_1,\ldots,A_m$ are independent of $\mathcal{D}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{D}_m$.
head: environment
name: Cluster-level randomization

label: rmk:within-cluster-subsampling
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:within-cluster-subsampling}
		We primarily consider the case in which the observed members in each cluster constitute the cluster's population of interest. In other cases, however, we may observe data from only $0<M_i\leq N_i$ units in cluster $i$, and the observed cluster size may depend on assignment and cluster-level attributes \citep{wang2024model}. That is, $M_i=A_iM_i(1)+(1-A_i)M_i(0)$ with $M_i(a)=h_a(N_i,\bm{C}_i,\epsilon_{a,i})$, where $h_a$ is a treatment-dependent unknown function and $\epsilon_i(a)$ is a treatment-dependent noise independent from $\{N_i,\bm{C}_i,\mathbf X_i,\mathbf Y_i(a)\}$. We refer to this setting as within-cluster subsampling and provide an extension of our main theoretical results under this setting in Section S8 of the Supplementary Materials.
head: environment

label: thm:np-est
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:np-est}
		Under Assumptions \ref{asp:sutva}-\ref{asp:cl-ran}, for $v=C,I$, if regularity conditions (P1)-(P4) in Section S1 of the Supplementary Materials hold, then $\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{np}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{\lambda}_v$; furthermore, if regularity conditions (P5)-(P7) also hold, then $m^{1/2}(\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{np}}-\bm{\lambda}_v)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}(\bm 0,\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{np}})$ and $\widehat \bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{np}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{np}}$.
head: environment

label: rmk:np-estimator
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:np-estimator}
		Our nonparametric estimators are connected with the two-sample U-statistics for clustered data, introduced in \citet{Lee2005}. To see this, we first asymmetrize \eqref{eq:np-equations} into $\sum_{1\leq i
eq k\leq m}\widetilde m{\psi}_v^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_i,\mathcal{O}_k; m{\lambda}) =  m 0$, where $\widetilde m{\psi}_v^{\mathrm{np}}=(\widetilde\psi_{v,1}^{\mathrm{np}},\widetilde\psi_{v,0}^{\mathrm{np}})$ for $v=C,I$, with $\widetilde\psi_{C,a}^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_i,\mathcal{O}_k;\lambda_a)=(N_iN_k)^{-1}\mathbbm{1}(A_i=a)\mathbbm{1}(A_k=1-a)\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}\sum_{l=1}^{N_k}\allowbreak\{w( m{Y}_{ij}, m{Y}_{kl})-\lambda_a\}$ and $\widetilde m{\psi}_I^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_i,\mathcal{O}_k; m{\lambda})=N_iN_k\widetilde m{\psi}_C^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_i,\mathcal{O}_k; m{\lambda})$, for $a\in\{0,1\}$. Then, for the cp-GCE, we have $\widehat\lambda_{C,a}^{\mathrm{np}}=\{m(m-1)\}^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i
eq k\leq m}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}\sum_{l=1}^{N_k}\phi_{C,a}^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{kl})$, where $\phi_{C,a}^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{kl})=(N_iN_k)^{-1}\mathbbm{1}(A_i=a)\mathbbm{1}(A_k=1-a)w( m{Y}_{ij}, m{Y}_{kl})$ and $\mathcal{O}_{ij}=\{ m{Y}_{ij},A_i,N_i,\allowbreak m{C}_i, m{X}_{ij}\}$. For the ip-GCE, we have $\widehat\lambda_{I,a}^{\mathrm{np}}=\{m(m-1)\}^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i
eq k\leq m}\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}\sum_{l=1}^{N_k}\phi_{I,a}^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{kl})$, where $\phi_{I,a}^{\mathrm{np}}(\mathcal{O}_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{kl})=\mathbbm{1}(A_i=a)\mathbbm{1}(A_k=1-a)w( m{Y}_{ij}, m{Y}_{kl})/[\{m(m-1)\}^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i
eq k\leq m}N_iN_k]$. Thus, both $\widehat\lambda_{C,a}^{\mathrm{np}}$ and $\widehat\lambda_{I,a}^{\mathrm{np}}$ take the form of clustered two-sample U-statistics given in \citet{Lee2005}.

label: thm:mr
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mr}
		Under Assumptions \ref{asp:sutva}-\ref{asp:cl-ran}, for $v=C,I$, if regularity conditions (P1)-(P4) in Section S1 of the Supplementary Materials hold, then $\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{mr}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{\lambda}_v$;, if regularity conditions (P5)-(P7) also hold, then $m^{1/2}(\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{mr}}-\bm{\lambda}_v)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}(\bm 0,\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{mr}})$ and $\widehat \bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{mr}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{mr}}$; these results hold regardless of the correct specification of the nuisance model $\zeta_a$. Moreover, if $\zeta_a(\underline\bm{\vartheta}_a)=\zeta_a^0$, then $\widehat \bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{mr}}$ converges in probability to the semiparametric efficiency lower bound of $\bm{\lambda}_v$.

label: thm:dml
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dml}
		Under Assumptions \ref{asp:sutva}-\ref{asp:cl-ran}, for $v=C,I$, if regularity conditions (C1)-(C5) in Section S5 of the Supplementary Materials hold, then $\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{dml}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{\lambda}_v$; additionally, if conditions (A1)-(A5) also hold, then $m^{1/2}(\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{\mathrm{dml}}-\bm{\lambda}_v)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}(\bm 0,\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{dml}})$; moreover, if (V1) also holds, then $\widehat \bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{dml}}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{dml}}$, where $\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{dml}}$ is the semiparametric efficiency lower bounds of $\bm{\lambda}_v$.

label: thm:incomplete
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:incomplete}
		Under Assumptions \ref{asp:sutva}-\ref{asp:cl-ran}, and regularity conditions listed in Sections S1 and Sections S5 of the Supplementary Materials, for ${\mathrm{est}}={\mathrm{np}},{\mathrm{mr}},{\mathrm{dml}}$ and $v=C,I$, $m^{1/2}(\widehat\bm{\lambda}_v^{{\mathrm{est}},*}-\bm{\lambda}_v)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}(\bm 0,\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{est}})$ and $\widehat\bm{V}_v^{{\mathrm{est}},\ast}\overset{p}{\to}\bm{V}_v^{\mathrm{est}}$, with $(\widehat V_v^{{\mathrm{est}},\ast})^{-1/2}(\widehat\Lambda_v^{{\mathrm{est}},\ast}-\Lambda_v)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

label: rmk:incomplete
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:incomplete}
		Results in Theorem \ref{thm:incomplete} are asymptotic based on the $m\to\infty$. In finite samples, however, losing $1-R^{-1}$ fraction of the pairs may result in efficiency loss as a tradeoff for computational efficiency. With small subsamples, finite-sample corrections \citep{MacKinnon1985} should be implemented to improve variance estimation. We demonstrate these observations in Section S7 of the Supplementary Materials.
head: environment
